artboards.title: As it stands today — thirteen faults, nine of them on the drawing
Proposed — the register of record, with four money columns that line up
Proposed — empty, the four marks, a name too long, and a read that failed
Proposed — the phone, drawn from scratch at 390

annotations.text:
WHAT YOU SETTLED, AND WHAT FOLLOWS FROM IT

I asked four questions before drawing. Everything here follows from your answers.

1. PRODUCTS IS THE REGISTER OF RECORD. You come here to set a line up and keep it right -- add it, name it, categorise it, photograph it, give it a markup rule -- not to browse. So the screen's first job is to tell you WHAT IS STILL UNFINISHED, and its second is to let you open any line in one click. Reading the catalogue is what the printed catalogue and the item picker are for.

2. DENSE ROWS, WITH A THUMBNAIL COLUMN. The photo stays, because two boxes of nails look identical in a list; it just stops leading. Four money columns run down the page in IBM Plex Mono, tabular, right-aligned, so what a line costs and what it fetches can be read against the line above it. That was impossible in a card grid and it is the whole reason for the change.

3. BOTH PRINT JOBS STAY VISIBLE. Print this list, the retail/wholesale selector, and Customer catalogue all sit in the header where they are now. The selector stays married to the Catalogue button, because the two bases produce different money on the same paper and a wholesale sheet handed to a walk-in customer undercharges every one of them.

4. CANVAS FIRST, THEN THE BUILD. Nothing in index.html has changed yet. What is here is the drawing; the conversion is the next step, and the last panel of this note lists what I have not decided for you.

THE ONE THING THAT IS A BUG WHATEVER YOU THINK OF THE DESIGN. Every card on the live screen reads "W +undefined% R +undefined%". There are two functions called markupRuleLabel in index.html -- one at line 53075 that handles the shop default correctly, and one at line 59724 that takes a rule OBJECT. The second shadows the first, so productLineHTML's call lands in the wrong one, rule.type is undefined, and it returns '+' + undefined + '%'. It has been on that screen for every product, all the time. It needs fixing whether or not you take any of this.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Inventory, Movements, the Price registry, Today, Debtors and Customers. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family. The photographs are grey placeholders; the real ones come from your media library.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS >

Drawn from the running app at 1440 with your own seeded price book. Nothing here is invented.

1. TWO PAGE TITLES, 74px APART. The header says "Products". Then a .panel-head-row says "ALL PRODUCTS". One screen, two headings, and the second carries no information at all.

2. THERE IS NO SUB-LINE. Every converted screen in the Catalogue group states in one line what it is -- Inventory: "What is on the shelf right now, what it cost, and what it is worth." Products says nothing and folds its whole explanation behind the "i". So the screen never introduces itself.

3. FOUR CONTROLS IN THE HEADER WITH NO ORDER OF IMPORTANCE. Print list, a select, Catalogue, Add product -- all 38px, all the same weight, spread across 563px. Three of them are the same job.

4. THE STRIP COUNTS THE WRONG THINGS. "0 without a price" and "6 not on the shelf" -- and both of those are questions Inventory owns and answers better. Nothing counts what this screen is for: how much of the register is actually finished.

5. AMBER ON SIX OF SIX. .sum-cell.warn paints "6 NOT ON THE SHELF" amber, and every line in this shop is not on the shelf. A mark that fires on everything marks nothing -- the same fault that got six card classes and their red left rails removed.

6. SIX EMPTY PHOTO FRAMES LEAD THE PAGE. The thumbnail takes the strongest position in every card and there is not one photograph on file. The screen's most prominent element is an absence.

7. TWENTY-EIGHT PIXEL EDIT AND DELETE, SIDE BY SIDE, TWELVE OF THEM. .pc-icon-btn is 28x28 against a 44px tap floor, and delete sits immediately beside edit on every card. At two hundred products that is four hundred controls, half of them destructive, on a list you thumb through in a yard.

8. THE CARDS ARE ALL DIFFERENT HEIGHTS, SO NOTHING CAN BE COMPARED. Iron Sheets' name runs to three lines; Steel Nails' category chip wraps and pushes its buttons down. The dashed line is drawn at the first card's "costs you" figure: the two beside it miss it by 15px and the fourth by 52px. A column of money that does not line up is unreadable at a glance, which is the only way a catalogue is read -- and in a grid there is no column at all.

9. "+undefined%" ON EVERY CARD, EVERY TIME. See the note on the left. This is the shadowed function, and it means the markup rule -- the one fact this screen owns that no other screen shows -- has never once been legible on it.

10. NOTHING SAYS WHICH LINE IS UNFINISHED. Not the strip, not the filters, not the cards. A product with no price, a product with no markup rule and a product whose variants were never built all look exactly like a finished one.

AND OFF THE DRAWING:

11. IT IS THE LAST LEGACY SCREEN IN ITS OWN GROUP. Inventory, Movements and the Price registry next door all speak .ow-ph / .ow-tb / .ow-pan / .ow-grid. Products still runs .page-head, .panel, .panel-head-row, .p-toolbar, .sum-strip.

12. THE RIGHT THIRD OF A 1440 SCREEN IS EMPTY. No rail, no context, and category -- a field on every single product, with sub-categories under it -- is not shown anywhere on the screen that owns it.

13. THE PHONE IS THE DESKTOP REFLOWED. About 700px of chrome -- three print controls, five stacked filters, a 2x2 strip -- before the first product. 820px is meant to be a switch between two designs, not one design narrowed.

THE PROPOSAL -- what changed, and why

THE STRIP COUNTS THE REGISTER'S CONDITION, NOT ITS MONEY. 23 products in 31 sellable lines; 4 not ready to sell; 12 of 31 with a photograph. Money is not in the strip at all, because what a line costs and fetches means nothing averaged -- it means something beside the line above it, which is what the four columns are for. Only one figure is coloured, and it is the only one that is a problem.

THE AMBER LINE IS THE SCREEN'S REASON TO EXIST, AND IT IS NOT THERE WHEN THERE IS NOTHING IN IT. "4 of 31 lines are not ready to sell. Two have no supplier price on file, one has no markup rule of its own and no shop default behind it, and one is sold in variants that have not been built yet." That sentence is a decomposition, not a badge: it says which three things are wrong and how many of each, so the count can be argued with. One line, one button, no banner.

THE ORDER IS NEWEST FIRST, WHICH IS NOT A COSMETIC CHOICE HERE. A line you added on Tuesday and did not finish is at the top of the screen on Wednesday. The register sorts itself into a to-do list without needing a to-do list.

FOUR MONEY COLUMNS THAT LINE UP. Costs you, Wholesale, Retail, On shelf. Under each figure the BASIS in 10.5px: "3 quotes - Mukwano", "default +15%", "+20% its own". So the screen finally shows the markup rule -- legibly, and distinguishing a rule the line sets for itself from the shop default it falls back on. That distinction is already in effectiveMarkupRule and has never been visible.

DASHES, NOT ZEROS, AND THE CHIP SAYS WHY ONCE. Wheelbarrow has no price, so its three money columns are dashes and its line carries one amber chip. Not a dash with an explanation under it AND a chip -- that is the same sentence twice on one row.

VARIANTS SIT UNDER THEIR PRODUCT. Iron Sheets is one grey band carrying the name, ID, category and photograph, and three variant rows under it carrying only what differs: the length, the code, and its own four figures. Today the full product name is repeated on every variant row.

THE ROW IS THE WAY IN, AND DELETE IS NOT ON THE LIST. One 52px row, one pencil at the end, and clicking anywhere on it opens the record. Deleting a product happens inside that record. That removes every 28px destructive button from the list -- at your seeded six products that is twelve controls gone, and at two hundred products it is four hundred.

THE RAIL IS THE SHAPE OF THE CATALOGUE. Seven categories with their sub-category counts, their line counts, and how many lines in each are unfinished -- clicking one filters the register. Under it, four doors to the screens that own the other half of the set-up (Media, the Price registry, What goes with what, Units and attributes) with their counts, and the shop's default markup stated in words. Not one figure in the rail is duplicated from another screen; they are counts and doors.

HEIGHT: the old screen spends its first 300px on a duplicate title, a strip that counts stock, and five filters. This one spends the same 300px on four figures about the register and one sentence naming everything that is unfinished in it.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. WHETHER "ON SHELF" BELONGS HERE AT ALL. You said this screen is for setting up and maintaining, and stock is Inventory's question -- I took it out of the strip on that reasoning. I kept it as a column because knowing a line is moving is useful when you are deciding whether its markup is worth arguing about. If you would rather it went entirely, that is 82px back to the name column.

2. WHAT "SET-UP" IN THE FILTER SHOULD OFFER. I have drawn it replacing today's "Pricing" filter, on the reasoning that "not priced yet" is one kind of unfinished and there are three. The options I would write are: Finished and not / Not ready to sell / No supplier price / No markup rule / No variants built / No photo. That last one is a real question ("what still needs photographing?") even though a missing photo is never a fault.

3. THE MARKUP COLUMNS SHOW ONE PRICE EACH. Wholesale and Retail each show the money and the rule that made it. What they do not show is the volume breaks -- your printed catalogue works those out and they can be substantial. I have left them off the register on the grounds that a break is a fact about a quantity, not about the line, but you may disagree.

4. WHETHER THE VARIANT GROUP HEADER IS RIGHT. The code emits no row for a variable product -- only its variants. I have drawn a grey band for the product anyway, so its name, ID, category and photo are said once instead of three times. It is presentation of the same data and the count is unchanged (31 lines either way), but it is the one place the drawing does not match the shape of productRowsForList.

5. THE PHONE HAS NO METRIC STRIP. The house pattern is 2x2 in one card, and I have drawn a single count line instead. My reasoning: at the desk you are auditing the register, in the yard you are finding one line, and 100px of condition figures is 100px not spent on the third product. The amber set-up line stays, because that one is worth a tap.

6. WHAT THE PHONE'S "PRINT" BUTTON OPENS. You said both print jobs stay. On the phone I have docked one Print control that opens a sheet asking retail or wholesale and which of the two documents -- rather than putting three controls in a 390px header. If you would rather the phone could not print at all, that is one button and the dock gets wider.

7. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED. productRowsForList, productLineStats, productBestBuy, suggestedSellingPrice, effectiveMarkupRule, the catalogue printer, the product form and its five panes, or any figure anywhere. This is the same data, computed the same way, drawn differently -- with one exception, which is the bug in the left-hand note.

8. AND THE BUG IS WORTH FIXING TODAY. Two functions named markupRuleLabel, the second shadowing the first, index.html lines 53075 and 59724. Say the word and it goes in as its own commit before any of this.

THE FOUR STATES

1. NOTHING IN THE REGISTER YET. The empty screen carries no strip, because four figures of zero are four figures that mean nothing. What it carries instead is the one sentence a new shop needs: a product is a name, a category and a markup rule, and everything else in the app hangs off it -- a supplier quote is a quote FOR a product, and so is a stock count, an order line and a row on the printed catalogue. One action, and a plain note that nothing else will appear until there is something to count.

2. WHAT "NOT READY TO SELL" MEANS, IN FOUR MARKS. Three causes, one amber chip, and each one says what clears it and where. No supplier price -- nothing has quoted it, so there is no cost to mark up. No markup rule -- it has a cost but nothing to turn into a price, and no shop default behind it either. No variants built -- sold in options that do not exist yet.

THE FOURTH LINE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. A MISSING PHOTO IS NOT A FAULT. It is counted in the strip and never chipped on a row. Nineteen of thirty-one lines have no photograph and four are genuinely unfinished; if the photo were a fault the amber would fire on two thirds of the register and stop meaning anything -- which is exactly what "6 NOT ON THE SHELF" does today.

3. A NAME LONGER THAN THE BOX IT WAS DRAWN FOR. The name column gives way with an ellipsis and carries the whole value in its tooltip; the basis line under a figure does the same. NO MONEY COLUMN EVER TRUNCATES -- the figure columns are sized to their content and the text gives way, because "1,240,00" is a tenth of "1,240,000" and looks entirely plausible. The same rule bars a bare input from holding a value that can outgrow it: an input clips mid-glyph with no ellipsis, no marker and no tooltip, which is how "Mulongo Hardware" once read as a different supplier on the quote screen.

4. THE PRICE BOOK DID NOT LOAD. This state does not exist today: if the read fails the screen shows zeros and a shop reads them as facts. Here the names, IDs and categories are shown because they read fine; every money column says "not read" rather than 0, because a zero would claim a line is free; and the set-up count is switched OFF rather than shown short, since it cannot know what is unfinished without the prices. Adding a product and editing a name still work -- those are writes to the register itself. Printing does not, and the two print buttons say why rather than producing a customer catalogue with every price missing.

THE PHONE -- its own design at 390

820px is a switch, so nothing here is the desktop narrowed. 44px navy bar, 26px Archivo page name, 15px body, targets over 44px, no fake status bar and no fake keyboard.

THE PHONE JOB IS NOT THE DESK JOB. At the desk you are working down the register deciding what still needs setting up. On a phone you are standing in front of the goods, or in front of a customer, and the question is WHICH LINE IS THIS. So: search first, full width, 48px, and photographs lead again -- on a 390px card a picture is the fastest way to tell 3 inch nails from 4 inch, and that is the one context where it beats a column.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. The five stacked filters (folded into one Filter control on the search bar). The four-tile strip (one count line instead -- see open question 5). And every button on every card: the whole card opens the record, which means there is no 28px delete under your thumb in a yard.

THE ACCENT IS IN THE THUMB ZONE, ONCE. A docked bar with Print and Add a product. Print opens a sheet that asks retail or wholesale and which document, rather than spending three controls of a 390px header on it.

THE UNFINISHED LINES STILL GET A LINE OF THEIR OWN, because it is worth a tap: "4 lines are not ready to sell. Two have no price, one no rule, one no variants."

A CARD THAT CANNOT BE PRICED SAYS SO INSTEAD OF SHOWING FIGURES. The wheelbarrow's card carries the amber chip and a sentence -- "Added 3 days ago. It cannot be quoted or catalogued until one supplier has priced it" -- where the two figures would be. Nothing on it is a zero.

THE TAB BAR. Five marks drawn for this shop rather than borrowed: a sunrise, a price tag, a note with a coin, a bubble speaking in figures, a stack of sheets. Active is FILLED and inactive is stroked, because a shape change reads at arm's length where a colour change alone does not.
